analysis.one_liner: Makes the 20% pass-through business tax deduction permanent.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 2 sponsors and 11 House Republican cosponsors, was referred to the Ways and Means Committee in June 2018 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the tax code to remove the expiration date on the qualified business income deduction created by the 2017 tax law. That deduction lets owners of pass-through businesses — partnerships, S corporations, LLCs, and sole proprietorships — deduct 20% of their business income before calculating tax. Without this bill, the deduction expires after 2025; with it, the deduction would be locked in permanently. The bill never moved after being referred to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of pass-through businesses, especially high-earning ones. The deduction only applies to business income, not wages, so its value rises with income. Independent analyses of the 2017 tax law's pass-through provision found the bulk of its benefit flowing to the top slice of earners, including owners of large partnerships in finance, real estate, and professional services.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the 2025 sunset on the 20% qualified business income deduction, giving pass-through owners a permanent 20% exclusion on their business income [S2][S3].
Gives business owners tax planning certainty; the bill's stated purpose is 'tax certainty' for these filers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, through a permanently smaller tax base. Revenue that would otherwise return to the Treasury when the deduction expires after 2025 instead stays with pass-through owners, increasing deficits or requiring offsetting taxes or cuts elsewhere.

drawbacks.text: Wage earners get no direct benefit: the deduction applies only to qualified business income, so salaried workers are excluded while high-earning business owners capture most of the value.

Making the deduction permanent forecloses the revenue that would return when the 2017 tax law's provision expires after 2025, adding to long-term deficits unless paid for with other tax increases or spending cuts.
Because the deduction's value scales with business income, permanent extension concentrates the benefit among the highest-earning business owners rather than typical small proprietorships.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some genuine small business owners would gain certainty about their tax rates, which the bill's sponsors emphasize. But the deduction is not targeted: it is available to any pass-through income, and its dollar value rises with income, so the largest permanent gains would go to owners of the largest and most profitable pass-through firms. The public cost is a permanently larger deficit or higher taxes elsewhere, with no direct benefit to the majority of households who earn wages.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in June 2018 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it; it died there when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Bishop of Michigan introduced the bill on June 28, 2018, joined by Rep. Erik Paulsen, to make the qualified business income deduction permanent [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5].
Eleven House Republicans cosponsored the bill [S4].
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action ever followed; the committee referral was the last entry in the bill's action history before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers are better off that the deduction was not made permanent, since the revenue it would forgone after 2025 stays in the Treasury. High-earning pass-through business owners are worse off only in the narrow sense that they did not get the permanence they sought; the deduction itself still exists under current law until its scheduled 2025 expiration.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal taxpayers; the deduction stays temporary

for.name: Rep. Mike Bishop
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the qualified business income deduction permanent.

for.name: Rep. Erik Paulsen
for.what_they_did: Joined Bishop in introducing the bill on June 28, 2018.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All listed supporters — the sponsor, the original cosponsor, and all 11 additional cosponsors — were Republicans, and no Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill.

industries.industry: Pass-through business owners (partnerships, S corporations, LLCs)
industries.note: The bill would lock in a permanent 20% deduction on their business income, a benefit unavailable to wage earners. Its dollar value scales with income, so the largest gains would go to the owners of the largest, most profitable pass-through firms, paid for through a smaller federal revenue base.

industries.industry: Large partnerships in finance, real estate, and professional services
industries.note: These firms generate the largest pass-through income streams and would capture the biggest absolute tax savings from a permanent deduction.
